title: Rapid versus gradual external ventricular drain weaning: a general review of best practices
condition_or_topic: Rapid versus gradual external ventricular drain (EVD) weaning in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH)
clinical_background: An EVD temporarily diverts cerebrospinal fluid to relieve hydrocephalus and elevated intracranial pressure. It is commonly used after aSAH, and up to 37% of these patients develop chronic hydrocephalus. EVD management may affect the need for a ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS), intensive care unit stay, and drain-related complications. Gradual weaning increases drainage resistance over several days, whereas rapid weaning closes the drain promptly. There is no consensus on which approach most safely permits EVD discontinuation while limiting VPS placement; the reported advantages and risks of each approach remain disputed.
objectives: Review the reported advantages and disadvantages of rapid and gradual EVD weaning to help reconcile differing views on clinical practice.
clinical_question: In patients with aSAH undergoing EVD weaning (Patient), how does rapid weaning (Intervention), compared with gradual weaning (Comparator), relate to VPS placement, infections, length of stay, and drain-related complications (Outcomes)?
study_design: Narrative literature review comparing rapid and gradual external ventricular drain (EVD) weaning; no formal review methodology is described.

population.description: Patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) receiving EVD management are the principal clinical population discussed.

interventions: Rapid EVD weaning: the drain is closed within 24 hours and reopened only for elevated ICP, neurological deterioration, or hydrocephalus or ventricular enlargement.
comparators: Gradual EVD weaning: drain height is raised by 5 cm every 24 hours to 25 cm H2O, followed by closure on day 4. Reopening is reserved for elevated ICP, neurological deterioration, or hydrocephalus or ventricular enlargement.
interpretation: The authors judge rapid EVD weaning to be preferable to gradual weaning for patients with aSAH, citing shorter ICU and hospital stays, less time with the drain in place, fewer drain failures and fewer infectious complications. They also associate rapid weaning with less frequent VPS placement, while acknowledging that studies disagree on shunt dependency and that most comparisons have not found a significant difference in infection rates.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: A survey conducted in 2017 found that 78% of participating institutions used gradual weaning. Evidence on shunt placement is mixed: one cited study reported placement rates of 13% with intermittent drainage and rapid weaning versus 35% with continuous drainage and gradual weaning, whereas a prospective RCT found no significant difference between approaches. A cited RCT involving 81 patients with aSAH reported that the gradual-weaning group averaged 2.8 more ICU days and 2.4 more hospital days than the rapid-weaning group. In a cited neonatal ICU study, average length of stay was 14.1 days with rapid weaning and 16.9 days with gradual weaning. A study of 200 patients with aSAH associated rapid weaning with shorter ICU and hospital stays and shorter mean EVD duration. One cited study found significantly more ventriculitis with gradual weaning, although other comparisons found no significant difference in infection rates.
clinical_implications: Shorter EVD duration and hospital stays with rapid weaning may reduce patients’ exposure to drain-related and hospital-related complications.
Ventriculitis may cause neurological deterioration, hydrocephalus or death if it is not adequately treated.

EVD failure can arise from mechanical problems, catheter obstruction or apparatus defects; the authors associate longer drain placement during gradual weaning with more opportunities for such problems.
The potential need for a VPS remains relevant whichever weaning strategy is used.
practice_implications: The authors recommend rapid rather than gradual EVD weaning as standard practice for patients with aSAH.
Clinicians should weigh complications alongside ICU and hospital length of stay, EVD duration and drain failure when choosing a weaning approach.
Clinicians should consider serious complications, including ventriculitis, meningitis, cerebral abscesses and subdural empyemas, when selecting an EVD weaning strategy.
limitations: The authors identify a shortage of multicenter prospective studies and state that much of the available RCT evidence comes from single centers, making its findings difficult to apply to larger populations.
open_questions: Which EVD weaning approach is definitively most effective and efficient remains unsettled, particularly given conflicting findings on subsequent shunt placement.
future_directions: The authors call for more multicenter prospective studies to establish the most effective and efficient EVD weaning approach.
main_conclusion: The authors conclude that rapid EVD weaning should replace gradual weaning as standard practice for patients with aSAH. They consider its reported advantages in hospital stay, drain-related complications and other outcomes to outweigh its risks.
narrative_summary:
This narrative review compares rapid and gradual external ventricular drain (EVD) weaning, particularly after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). Gradual weaning progressively raises the drain before closure on day 4; rapid weaning closes it within 24 hours. The authors assess shunt placement, infection, drain function and length of stay using findings from published studies rather than a new patient cohort.

The cited evidence is mixed on ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) dependency. One study’s multivariate analysis favored gradual weaning, whereas a comparison of intermittent drainage with rapid weaning against continuous drainage with gradual weaning reported shunt insertion rates of 13% and 35%, respectively. A cited randomized trial found no significant difference in shunt placement between approaches. Infection findings also differ: some studies favor rapid weaning, but the review notes that comparisons have often found no statistically significant difference.

Length of stay more consistently favors rapid weaning. In a cited trial involving 81 patients with aSAH, the gradual-weaning group averaged 2.8 more days in the ICU and 2.4 more days in the hospital. Another cited study reported non-functioning EVD rates of 15% with rapid weaning and 30% with gradual weaning. The authors favor rapid weaning in clinical practice while acknowledging that the shortage of multicenter prospective studies limits certainty about the best protocol.

document_sections.heading: Rapid versus gradual external ventricular drain weaning: a general review of best practices
document_sections.content: The choice between rapid and gradual external ventricular drain (EVD) weaning remains disputed because each approach has potential benefits and risks. Some published studies favor gradual weaning for its perceived ability to reduce ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) dependence. Rapid weaning has been associated with fewer ventriculostomy-related infections, whereas gradual weaning may prolong hospitalization. This literature review examines arguments for and against both approaches. The authors conclude that rapid weaning offers more consistent benefits and fewer overall risks, and should become standard practice for patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: An EVD removes cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to relieve hydrocephalus and elevated intracranial pressures (ICP). It is often used after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH); up to 37% of these patients develop chronic hydrocephalus, many remain in the intensive care unit (ICU) for extended periods, and a substantial number require permanent CSF diversion through a VPS. EVD management can affect VPS requirements, ICU stay and drain-related complications. There is no consensus on which discontinuation strategy is safest or least likely to require a VPS. Gradual weaning increases drainage resistance over several days; rapid weaning closes the EVD promptly. In the described gradual protocol, drain height rises by 5 cm every 24 hours to 25 cm H2O, followed by closure on day 4. The drain is usually reopened only for ICP >20 cm H2O for 5 minutes, clinical neurological deterioration, or hydrocephalus or ventricular enlargement on the following day's computed tomography brain scan. Rapid weaning closes the drain within 24 hours, with reopening under the same stated conditions; the rapid-protocol description gives the ICP threshold as >20 cm. Elevated ICP is a common reason for EVD use, alongside consideration of compliance, hemodynamic strain and metabolic dysfunction. Reduced intracranial compliance, meaning reduced capacity of the cranial vault to accommodate increased volume, indicates elevated ICP. The article describes the EVD as useful for assessing intracranial compliance and for delivering intrathecal drugs, including antibiotics and thrombolytics, as well as draining CSF. The literature has not settled which weaning method is safest and most effective. Advocates of gradual weaning cite a possible reduction in shunt dependence without greater infection risk; others regard the methods as having comparable benefits and risks. Proponents of rapid weaning cite possible reductions in meningitis, ventriculitis, other infections, hospital stay and costs, together with better ventricular compliance. Current Neurocritical Care Society guidance recommends completing EVD weaning as quickly as the patient's clinical condition permits to limit monitoring duration and ventriculostomy-related infection risk. VPS requirement is central to the disagreement because permanent diversion can itself cause complications, including pseudocysts, perforations and hernias. Published studies disagree on whether gradual or rapid weaning lowers shunt dependence after aSAH. The authors therefore call for an agreed, explicitly defined standard approach.

document_sections.heading: GRADUAL WEANING
document_sections.content: The best way to manage EVDs after acute subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) remains disputed. EVDs have been used for acute SAH for over 50 years, and many institutions have traditionally chosen gradual weaning. Emerging research suggests that this longstanding choice is not necessarily superior.

document_sections.heading: Pros
document_sections.content: A cited multivariate analysis found less shunt dependence among patients undergoing gradual rather than rapid weaning. That study found no significant between-method difference in symptomatic vasospasm or ventriculostomy-associated infections. Another cited trial reported a longer length of stay (LOS) with gradual weaning, but its findings were not significant and did not favor either approach. Keeping the EVD longer may offer flexibility: many physicians prefer it to remain in place during the vasospasm period after aSAH, and gradual adjustment allows its duration to be managed until weaning is complete.

document_sections.heading: Cons
document_sections.content: Cited research has associated gradual weaning with a significant increase in hospital LOS relative to rapid weaning. Longer hospitalization is linked to higher mortality, worse patient outcomes and substantial costs for patients and hospitals. Longer EVD placement may also increase complications and drain malfunction. The study reporting less shunt dependence with gradual weaning additionally found that incremental weaning was more likely to be followed by secondary shunt placement after an initially successful wean, further prolonging hospitalization. The authors state that this secondary shunt risk calls for adequate neurological care after discharge. Although gradual weaning remains standard in most institutions, evidence of possible complications may favor a shift toward rapid weaning.

document_sections.heading: RAPID WEANING
document_sections.content: The authors present rapid weaning as a possible alternative to the traditionally preferred gradual approach. In one cited comparison, intermittent drainage with rapid weaning had a shunt insertion rate of 13%, versus 35% with continuous drainage and gradual weaning; the study reported a significant reduction. Multiple cited studies found that rapid weaning significantly shortened ICU and overall hospital LOS. One cited study also reported non-functioning EVD rates of 15% with rapid weaning and 30% with gradual weaning. Rapid weaning may improve the likelihood of successful drain removal. Earlier removal can shorten EVD use and ICU and hospital stays without harming safety or clinical outcomes. One study suggested that rapid weaning could lower ventriculostomy-associated infection risk. A multicenter observational study across six United States neurocritical care units associated rapid weaning with fewer EVD complications, an ICU LOS shorter by approximately 2.1 days, and less shunt placement. Nevertheless, complications remain possible. Despite an individual report of fewer ventriculostomy-associated infections, the majority consensus described here finds no significant infection benefit for rapid versus gradual weaning. Rapid weaning may increase shunt dependence, although most cited studies found non-significant differences in shunt dependence between approaches.

document_sections.heading: POTENTIAL CHALLENGES IN GRADUAL VERSUS RAPID WEANING
document_sections.content: Shunt placement remains a possible outcome with either protocol: a patient unable to tolerate EVD weaning will require a shunt. A cited prospective randomized control trial (RCT) found no significant difference in shunt placement between treatment approaches, whereas a multicenter study associated rapid weaning with less shunt placement. This conflict limits certainty. Longer EVD placement has been linked to more unwanted outcomes, including infection and recurrent hydrocephalus. By potentially shortening placement, rapid weaning could reduce ICU complications such as hemorrhage, meningitis, ventriculitis, brain abscess, empyema and dislodgement. However, comparisons of weaning protocols have not shown a statistically significant difference in infection rates. The authors identify a shortage of multicenter prospective studies as a major obstacle to establishing best practice. Most available RCTs were conducted at single centers, limiting how readily their findings apply to larger populations. The authors call for additional multicenter prospective studies to determine the most effective and efficient approach.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: Gradual weaning has long been favored, partly because of a presumed lower risk of shunt dependence and possible reluctance to adopt rapid weaning. In a 2017 survey, 78% of participating institutions used gradual weaning. The authors argue that customary preference does not necessarily establish superiority and that clinicians should weigh complications and outcomes for both methods. They consider rapid weaning a promising approach with comparatively few risks and generally favor it because they judge its complication burden to be lower. Ventriculitis is a CSF infection in the ventricles and a possible EVD-related complication. A cited 2020 study supported by the American Heart Association, American Stroke Association, and National Institutes of Health found significantly higher infection rates with gradual than with rapid weaning. Untreated ventriculitis can lead to neurological deterioration, hydrocephalus and death. The authors also identify meningitis, cerebral abscesses and subdural empyemas as serious complications associated with gradual weaning and advise clinicians to consider these risks when choosing an approach. Relevant outcomes include hospital LOS, ICU/Neuro ICU LOS, total EVD duration and EVD failure rate; shorter hospitalization can also reduce hospital-related complications and costs. In a cited RCT of 81 patients with aSAH, the gradual-weaning group spent an average of 2.8 more days in the ICU and 2.4 more days in the hospital than the rapid-weaning group. A cited neonatal ICU study reported an average LOS of 14.1 days with rapid weaning and 16.9 days with gradual weaning. In another cited study of 200 patients with aSAH who received EVDs, rapid weaning was associated with shorter ICU and hospital LOS and a shorter mean EVD duration; the study linked the shorter duration to a substantial reduction in ventriculostomy-associated infection risk. The authors interpret shorter stays and their consequences as favoring the efficiency of rapid weaning. EVDs can fail because of mechanical problems, catheter obstruction or apparatus defects. The authors state that failure is more frequent with gradual weaning because the drain stays in place for 4 days or more, allowing more opportunities for problems such as twisted tubing or apparatus displacement. They contrast this with removal within 24 hours under rapid weaning and its association with substantially fewer non-functioning EVDs. Overall, the authors favor rapid weaning for what they describe as fewer infectious complications and improved outcomes through shorter ICU and hospital stays, less time with an EVD, and fewer EVD failures.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: The authors conclude that rapid weaning is the more effective and efficient EVD strategy in numerous clinical situations. They associate it with a lower overall VPS placement rate, shorter hospitalization, fewer drain complications, better functional outcomes and improved ventricular compliance. They also cite fewer EVD failures, lower infection risk and a greater likelihood of successful drain removal. In their assessment, these benefits appear more consistently than those of gradual weaning and outweigh rapid weaning's risks. They argue that the continued institutional preference for gradual weaning often conflicts with the approach they consider more effective. Although they describe a growing shift away from gradual weaning, their final recommendation is specifically that rapid rather than gradual weaning should become standard clinical practice for EVD management in patients with aSAH.
